prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Why hast thou nothing in thy face? Thou idol of the human race, Thou tyrant of the human heart, The flower of lovely youth that art; Yea, and that standest in thy youth An image of eternal Truth, With thy exuberant flesh so fair, That only Pheidias might compare, Ere from his chaste marmoreal form Time had decayed the colours warm; Like to his gods in thy proud dress, Thy starry sheen of nakedness. Surely thy body is thy mind, For in thy face is nought to find, Only thy soft unchristen’d smile, That shadows neither love nor guile, But shameless will and power immense, In secret sensuous innocence. O king of joy, what is thy thought? I dream thou knowest it is nought, And wouldst in darkness come, but thou Makest the light where’er thou go. Ah yet no victim of thy grace, None who e’er long’d for thy embrace, Hath cared to look upon thy face.

outputs.L1:
This is already a finely wrought piece of verse, rich in classical allusion and Victorian-style diction. Since it is poetry—governed by meter, rhyme, and archaic voice by design—I've limited my edits to smoothing a few syntactically awkward moments while preserving every image, idea, and word choice, as well as the rhyme scheme and elevated tone throughout.

---

Why hast thou nothing in thy face,
Thou idol of the human race,
Thou tyrant of the human heart,
Fair flower of youth, thou truly art;
Yea, standing still within thy youth,
An image of eternal Truth,
With thy exuberant flesh so fair
That only Pheidias might compare,
Ere from his chaste and marmoreal form
Time had decayed the colours warm;
Like to his gods in thy proud dress,
Thy starry sheen of nakedness.
Surely thy body is thy mind,
For in thy face is nought to find,
Only thy soft unchristen'd smile,
That shadows neither love nor guile,
But shameless will and power immense,
In secret, sensuous innocence.
O king of joy, what is thy thought?
I dream thou knowest it is nought,
And fain in darkness wouldst thou go,
Yet light attends thee even so.
Ah yet no victim of thy grace,
None who hath longed for thy embrace,
Hath ever cared to see thy face.

---

**Notes on the light revisions made:**
- *"The flower of lovely youth that art"* → *"Fair flower of youth, thou truly art"* — resolves the awkward inverted syntax while preserving meaning and rhyme.
- *"Yea, and that standest in thy youth"* → *"Yea, standing still within thy youth"* — smooths the clunky double conjunction.
- *"And wouldst in darkness come, but thou / Makest the light where'er thou go"* → *"And fain in darkness wouldst thou go, / Yet light attends thee even so"* —
outputs.L2:
Why does thy countenance hold nothing at all?
Thou, worshipped by all mankind,
Thou who rules over every heart,
The very essence of beautiful youth;
Indeed, standing there in thy prime,
A living picture of everlasting Truth,
With such rich, radiant flesh
That only Pheidias could rival it,
Before time faded the warm hues
From his pure marble sculptures;
Like his deities in thy magnificent form,
Thy brilliant, unclothed splendor.

Surely thy essence lies within thy form,
For thy expression reveals nothing,
Save thy gentle, unconsecrated grin,
Which betrays neither affection nor deceit,
But rather brazen will and vast strength,
Held within a private, sensual purity.

O sovereign of delight, what occupies thy mind?
I suspect thou knowest it holds nothing,
And would prefer to dwell in shadow, yet
Light follows wherever thou walkest.

Still, not one who fell prey to thy charm,
Not one who ever craved thy touch,
Has troubled to gaze upon thy face.
outputs.L3:
# The Idol of Flesh: An Analysis of Beauty Without Depth

The poem presents its subject—a youth of extraordinary physical perfection—not merely as an object of admiration but as something approaching religious devotion. He is cast as an idol, a figure before whom human hearts kneel in worship, and simultaneously as a tyrant, one who exercises a kind of dominion over those who behold him. This duality is central to the poem's vision: beauty here is both worshipped and feared, adored and obeyed. The youth becomes a living embodiment of eternal beauty and truth, as though his very existence proves that such ideals can take physical form, however fleeting the vessel that houses them may ultimately be.

To capture the extraordinary nature of his physical form, the poem invokes the sculptural genius of Pheidias, the great Athenian artist whose works defined classical notions of ideal human beauty. This comparison elevates the youth beyond mere mortal handsomeness into the realm of timeless art—suggesting that his form possesses the same untouchable perfection as marble statuary, a beauty that seems to exist outside the corrosive effects of age and decay. Yet this comparison carries an implicit irony: statues, however beautiful, are also cold, static, and lifeless in their perfection.

This irony deepens as the poem turns from the youth's body to his mind, only to suggest that there is, in truth, no meaningful distinction between the two. His face, for all its radiance, betrays no hidden depths, no complexity of thought or feeling. What one finds instead is an innocent smile—untouched by the sophistication of Christian understanding, unmarked by love, and equally free of guile or deception. This is not the smile of someone concealing profound emotion; it is the smile of someone who simply has nothing to conceal, because there is nothing beneath the surface to hide.

The poem thus constructs a startling paradox: this youth, who seems to radiate an almost divine light capable of illuminating darkness itself, harbors thoughts that are essentially "nought"—empty, insubstantial, without meaning or weight. His brilliance is entirely surface-level, a luminosity that dazzles the eye while offering nothing to the mind or soul. He shines, but he does not illuminate in any deeper sense; his presence brightens a room without ever enlightening those within it.

Perhaps most striking is the poem's final observation about those who desire this youth. Despite—or perhaps because of—his emptiness, he continues to attract worship and longing. Yet the poem notes with pointed irony that his admirers never actually care to look upon his face, to seek out whatever expression or meaning might be found there. Their desire is fixed entirely upon his body, his physical form, with no genuine interest in connection, understanding, or intimacy of a deeper kind. This final paradox completes the poem's meditation on beauty: it can inspire devotion and desire while remaining fundamentally isolating, prized precisely because it demands nothing more than the pleasure of the gaze.
outputs.L4:
# Untitled Reflection on Divine Beauty

The poem opens with an invocation to a young man whose physical beauty transcends mortal description, positioning him alongside the great works of Pheidias, the legendary Greek sculptor whose statues of gods and heroes defined the classical ideal of physical perfection. This comparison immediately elevates the youth beyond ordinary human categories—he is not merely handsome but statuesque, godlike, a living embodiment of the same aesthetic principles that guided ancient sculptors in their attempts to capture divine form in marble and bronze.

The speaker lingers on the youth's face, describing features that seem to glow with an almost supernatural radiance. Yet as the poem progresses, a curious tension emerges: despite this loving, almost worshipful attention to physical detail, the speaker begins to probe beneath the surface, asking what lies behind those perfect features. What thoughts occupy this beautiful mind? What emotions flicker behind that radiant expression? The poem suggests an emptiness or fundamental unknowability at the core of this figure—as though his beauty exists almost independently of any interior life, or as though that interior life is simply inaccessible, veiled by the very perfection that makes him so captivating.

This inquiry leads to the poem's central and most provocative revelation: those who are drawn to the youth, who desire him, who admire him from afar or up close, never actually attempt to understand what he thinks or feels. His beauty is so complete, so overwhelming in its self-sufficiency, that it seems to preclude the need for deeper knowledge. Admirers are content merely to look, to admire, to desire—the physical form alone satisfies whatever longing draws them to him. The poem thus suggests a troubling truth about the nature of desire and physical perfection: that overwhelming beauty can render questions of character, intellect, or inner truth not just secondary but entirely unnecessary. The youth becomes, in effect, a beautiful surface without an interior that matters to those who love him—not because he lacks depth, but because his beauty makes that depth irrelevant to the transactional nature of admiration and desire.

In this way, the poem meditates on the strange alienation that can accompany extraordinary physical beauty, suggesting that those who are most looked at may paradoxically be the least truly seen or known.
outputs.L5:
# Why, Thou, The

There is a peculiar power in fragments. Three words—*why*, *thou*, *the*—seem incomplete alone, yet together they gesture toward something larger: a question, an address, a pointing finger toward specificity in a world drowning in vagueness.

**Why** is perhaps humanity's oldest word, though it rarely appears first in any language's vocabulary. Children ask it before they can spell it. Philosophers spend lifetimes chasing its tail. *Why* is the wound that never quite closes—why suffering, why beauty, why anything at all rather than nothing? It is a word that refuses satisfaction. Every answer to *why* births another *why*, an infinite regression that either drives us mad or drives us toward wonder, depending on our temperament.

**Thou** belongs to an older register of speech, intimate in a way "you" has lost. It appears in prayers, in love poems, in accusations hurled at the heavens. To say *thou* is to address something directly, without the buffer of formality—it collapses distance. When someone writes "Why hast thou forsaken me," the word does double work: it is both plea and indictment, question and relationship, all bound into a single syllable that insists on presence, on being spoken *to* rather than merely *about*.

**The** is the humblest word of the three, and perhaps the most philosophically loaded. It is the definite article—the tool language uses to say: not just any, but *this one*, *the specific one*, *the only one that matters here*. "The" transforms abstraction into particularity. It is the difference between *a* truth and *the* truth, between *a* answer and *the* answer we've been seeking.

Placed together, these three words form something like a skeleton of longing: *Why* [have] *thou* [forsaken] *the* [one who loved you]? Or simply: the eternal human posture of questioning something specific, someone particular, some absence keenly felt.

Language, at its barest, is built from such small words—the hinges on which larger meanings swing. *Why*, *thou*, and *the* are not grand nouns or vivid verbs; they carry no imagery of their own. Yet without them, we could not ask, could not address, could not specify. They are the grammar of longing itself: the eternal question, spoken to someone, about the one thing that matters.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style poem in archaic English addressing a beautiful youth as an "idol" whose face reveals nothing behind his physical perfection, with classical allusions to Greek sculpture like Pheidias.
counterfactuals.output:
**To an Idol**

Thou art an idol wrought in living stone,
As Pheidias once shaped the brow of Zeus—
A beauty absolute, and thine alone,
That asks no reverence, yet compels its use.

I search thy face as one who scans the skies
For some lone star to name, some secret sign,
But find no more within thy lucent eyes
Than in the sculptured eyes of gods divine.

As once the gold and ivory did compose
Athena's form beneath the Parthenon's shade,
So doth thy flesh, in perfect line, disclose
A loveliness no less serenely made.

What god, I ask, doth dwell behind thy brow?
What soul lies chambered in that noble frame?
Perchance none dwells—I cannot fathom how
A face so fair should hold nor joy nor shame.

For statues feel not, though the sculptor's art
Doth lend them breath enough to mock our tears;
And thou, dear idol, hast perchance no heart,
But only beauty's silence down the years.

Yet still I kneel, though I should kneel to nought
But marble calm that masks the empty air—
For beauty, self-sufficient, needeth not
To be redeemed by aught, save being fair.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical ode using "thou" and "thy" that explores the tension between physical beauty and emptiness of expression, invoking marble statues and eternal Truth.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ode to the Marble Silence

Thou standest, carved in cold perfection's line,
Thy brow unbent by sorrow, joy, or care,
A form that mortal hands could scarce design,
Yet what dost thou, О silent one, declare?

Thy marble flesh knows neither blush nor tear,
Thy lips, though shaped for song, have never sung,
Thou art the image beauty holds most dear,
But silence dwells where should have dwelt a tongue.

I gaze upon thy flawless, sculpted face
And wonder if thy heart of stone can feel
The ancient ache that time cannot erase—
Or art thou beauty's mask that guards the real?

For Truth, they say, in beauty makes her home,
Yet thou art beauty stripped of Truth's own fire;
Thou art the temple with an empty dome,
The unstrung harp that cannot touch the lyre.

What good thy grace, thy form so well arrayed,
If nothing stirs behind thy sightless eyes?
Thou art a promise time has not delayed
But one that never ripens, never dies.

Yet still I linger, drawn by thy cold grace,
For even emptiness can teach us this:
That beauty void of soul, though fair its face,
Is but a shadow of eternal bliss.

Speak, marble form, though thou hast never spoken—
Thy silence is itself a kind of Truth:
That beauty, when the vessel lies unbroken,
May hide the very absence of its youth.

So let me learn from thee, thou voiceless stone,
That Truth needs more than beauty to be whole—
Thy perfect form, forever cold, alone,
Reminds me beauty starves without a soul.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem in the style of 19th-century aestheticism about a strikingly beautiful but vacant-faced young man, described as godlike, sensuous, and dangerously alluring.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Marble Youth

In gardens where the languid roses fall,
He stands, a thing too beautiful for thought,
His marble brow beneath the cypress-wall
Where centuries of longing have been wrought.

O face that Phidias might have carved in dream!
The curve of lip that knows not what it means,
Those eyes like still, cold pools where shadows seem
To move—yet nothing living intervenes.

His throat's pale column, and the golden hair
That falls in ringlets like some captured light,
Speak of a beauty terrible to bear,
A loveliness too perfect, too polite

To hold within it any human spark.
He is a god who has forgotten why
The ancients raised him, standing in the dark
Perfection of an unrecorded sky.

I would not have him speak, for should he speak
The spell might break upon some foolish word—
Better this silence, dangerous and bleak,
Than hear a mind as shallow as a bird's.

Yet still I burn. Such danger draws me on—
The moth knows well the candle's cruel light,
And I, poor fool, would rather be undone
By loveliness than saved by something right.

He does not know the ruin that he makes
Of hearts that pass too near his radiant form;
Vacant as marble, he feels not the aches
Of those who perish, wanting to be warm

Against a beauty that can never warm
Them back, that only wants itself, alone—
A sculptured plague, a sweet and lovely storm,
A living, breathing, thoughtless thing of stone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhymed, iambic poem addressing an idealized male figure whose beauty is compared to ancient Greek statuary, exploring themes of innocence, power, and the absence of moral depth behind a perfect face.
counterfactuals.output:
**Statuary**

You stand as if Praxiteles had dreamed
you whole from marble warmed to living stone—
the throat, the brow, the shoulder's line that seemed
too pure for flesh, too perfect to be your own.

No shadow crosses that untroubled face,
no history has carved a single line;
you wear your beauty like a borrowed grace,
unearned, unquestioned, radiantly benign.

The gods who shaped you never gave you good—
only the shape that good wears when it's young.
You move through rooms the way a statue would:
admired, untouched, and quietly among

a power that you never had to earn.
Men look at you and think that they have seen
some deeper truth, some soul they can discern,
when all they've found's the polish of the sheen.

Innocence, they call it—call it blank,
the smooth unwritten surface of a stone.
What lies beneath that pedestal and rank
is neither dark nor bright—it is unknown.

Achilles had his wrath, his human flaw;
you have a face that asks for nothing back.
The beautiful are seldom bound by law—
the world forgives the thing it does not lack.

So stand there, marble boy, and let them stare,
let poets raise you temples out of rhyme.
Someday the years will find you unaware
and give at last what beauty spared: real time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an archaic-toned love poem meditating on a youth so physically radiant that no one who desires him dares look upon his face, blending classical imagery with themes of sensuous innocence and hidden emptiness.
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon One Too Fair to Behold**

Lo, what a boy the elder gods have wrought,
and set among us mortals as a snare—
his brow more bright than any dawn hath brought,
his throat the pale of lilies drowned in air.
No man that loves him dares to lift his eyes
unto that face, as none dared look on old
upon the naked splendor of the skies
when Semele was ash before she told
her longing to the thunderer. So we,
who burn for him, do turn our gaze aside,
and worship at the hem, and bend the knee,
and drink him sidelong, as the sea drinks tide—
  for straight to face him were to face the sun,
  and none has looked unblinded, only one.

They say Narcissus perished of his pool,
enamored of a shadow, not a form—
but this boy needs no water to be fool
unto himself; he is his own mild storm,
so brimmed with beauty that he cannot spill
one drop of it toward those who ache and wait.
Ganymede was borne off 'gainst his will
to pour out wine at Jove's undying gate—
but this one pours out nothing. He is cup
and vacancy together, gold and void,
a vessel lifted, luminous, held up
to lips that tremble, thirsting, and destroyed
  not by refusal, nor by cruelty,
  but by the hollow at his heart's own sea.

Ah, sweet unfinished innocence, that wears
its emptiness as roses wear the dew—
he does not know what ruin he prepares
for those who study him the whole night through.
Adonis bled and something still was lost;
this boy sheds nothing, for he holds no wound.
His beauty is a winter without frost,
a bell whose silver throat gives forth no sound.
We love the ringing that we do not hear,
we love the wound that never once drew blood,
we love, and loving, dare not draw too near,
lest, like Actaeon in the sacred wood,
  our own desire should tear us into four
  and scatter us as leaves upon his floor.

Yet still I come at dusk to where he stands
half-lit by lantern and by rising moon,
and I do offer him my empty hands,
and I do hum some old, unfinished tune—
not hoping he will turn his face to mine,
for I have heard what happens to the bold,
but only that I might, like bread and wine,
be blessed a little by the way he holds
himself apart, a god who does not know
he wears divinity as one wears skin.
I do not ask the fire's steady glow
to warm the small and human house within—
  I ask to kneel where he has stood, and feel
  the absence of his hand, which was not real.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
